analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue gun makers and sellers by repealing their legal liability shield.
analysis.headline: The bill to let gun violence victims sue manufacturers has 114 House cosponsors, all Democrats, and has not advanced past committee since it was referred on June 4, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 2005, a federal law called the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act has blocked most lawsuits against gun and ammunition makers, dealers, and trade groups for harm caused by the criminal or unlawful use of a firearm. This bill repeals that shield, so a person injured or a family that lost someone could take the industry to court like victims of any other product can. It also makes federal gun-trace data usable as evidence in those lawsuits, so courts could see where a gun came from and how it moved through the market.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or families of those killed in shootings, who today have almost no way to sue manufacturers, sellers, or dealers over how a gun reached a shooter. Communities harmed by illegal gun trafficking also benefit, because trace data showing the source of crime guns would become available in court.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, the 2005 federal law that prohibits civil suits against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm.

Makes the ATF's Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoena and discovery, admissible as evidence, and usable in any state or federal civil action or administrative proceeding, letting plaintiffs show where a crime gun came from and how it reached the shooter.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, and trade associations, which would face civil liability for the unlawful use of their products and would bear the cost of litigation, settlements, and likely higher liability insurance. Gun buyers could see some of those costs passed through in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade groups

drawbacks.text: The bill exposes an entire lawful industry to lawsuits over crimes committed by third parties who misused a legal product, which critics argue holds sellers responsible for acts they did not commit and is unlike the treatment of most other products that are lawful to sell.

Litigation risk for manufacturers and dealers could raise prices and push smaller dealers out of the market, costs that would partly fall on lawful gun buyers, and repeal could revive the wave of lawsuits the 2005 law was passed to stop.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and specific: victims today are nearly locked out of the courthouse because of a single federal statute, and this bill restores their ability to sue and to see trace evidence. The cost is genuine too, since a liability regime for criminal misuse by third parties is a heavier burden than most industries bear and would likely be passed on to buyers. Weighing those, the bill gives a concrete legal remedy to people who suffered injury that courts cannot currently touch, at the price of a large, largely hypothetical cost spread across a lawful industry and its customers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Swalwell introduced the bill on June 4, 2025, joined by 114 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day and has had no further action, with no markup or floor vote scheduled.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations remain protected by the 2005 liability shield, since the bill has not moved, and their current position is unchanged. Victims of gun violence remain unable to sue them over criminal misuse of a firearm.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The gun industry's liability shield stands

for.name: Rep. Eric Swalwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 114 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 114 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, no action taken
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 4, 2025 and has not scheduled a markup or taken any action on it since.

against.name: Firearms industry and trade associations
against.role: Industry protected by the law the bill would repeal
against.what_they_did: The bill would strip the industry's federal liability shield, and the industry and its trade groups have long opposed repealing the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act.

sides.party_line_note: All 114 cosponsors are Democrats and there is no Republican support on the bill; Republicans control the House and the Judiciary Committee that would have to move it.

industries.industry: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill repeals the 2005 federal shield that blocks lawsuits against the industry for the criminal or unlawful misuse of its products, exposing it to civil damages suits. That shield is the reason victims currently cannot recover from manufacturers, so the industry's protection comes directly at the public's expense in court.

industries.industry: National Trace Center of the ATF (government database)
industries.note: The bill removes the protection that keeps federal gun-trace data out of court proceedings, making the Firearms Trace System database discoverable and admissible in civil suits. This helps plaintiffs rather than the agency, which is why the agency's data interest runs opposite to its usual position.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and a Republican-controlled House and Judiciary Committee, the bill is very unlikely to receive a markup or floor vote this Congress. The most likely path is that it sits in committee until the session ends, as prior attempts to repeal the 2005 liability shield have done in similarly divided Congresses.
